To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the debt to equity ratio, proportion of outside directors, large blockholder presence and adviser structure affect earnings management around UK Rights issues.
firms with lower debt-to-equity ratios, a higher proportion of outside directors, or a large blockholder are less likely to use discretionary accruals to manage earnings around rights issues.

firms with higher levels of leverage, with lower proportions on non-executive directors and with no large blockholder, are more likely than other firms to use discretionary current accural to manipulate earnings around their rights issues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a specific corporate event (rights issues), which has not been investigated before, and is based on a unique data set of UK firms.
the role of corporate governance mechanisms in preventing opportunistic earnings management.
the role of corporate governance in mitigating the potential for earnings management around UK corporate events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UK corporate governance mechanisms do not appear to be effective in reducing earnings management around rights issues, but that the evidence is mixed.
the corporate governance mechanisms are not working effectively to control earnings management around UK equity offerings.
the UK corporate governance system is effective at preventing opportunistic earnings management.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
firms with higher leverage, lower non-executive director representation, or without a large blockholder, are more likely than other firms to manipulate earnings around UK rights issues.
the more corporate governance is present, the less earnings management occurs.
the UK market is still not immune to opportunistic earnings management, and that the current corporate governance mechanisms do not appear to be effective in checking earnings management.
The main takeaway from our work is that
investors should be cautious when evaluating the earnings of firms with poor corporate governance structures, especially around rights issues.
investors can rely on financial disclosures of firms that have a low debt to equity ratio, a high proportion of independent directors, and a large blockholder.
firms with higher levels of debt, lower proportions of outside directors and with no large blockholder are more likely to engage in opportunistic earnings management.
